Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

Scaling laws ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) motivate larger models for improved quality, while their memory and computational demands increase reliance on cloud infrastructure with high-end accelerators. However, network connectivity can be unstable in underwater and rescue operations ( Stojanovic & Preisig, 2009 ; Deng et al., 2013 ; Gunn & Anderson, 2015 ) . Safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving require on-device decisions to avoid cloud communication delays ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Kuutti et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Bodmer et al., 2026 ) , while privacy requirements can prevent sensitive data from being uploaded ( European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016 ; Shi et al., 2016 ) . These constraints require large-model inference to move from the cloud to resource-constrained edge devices. Fitting large models within limited memory and achieving low inference latency with the available computational resources are the two critical challenges of this transition. The latency requirement is particularly important in feedback control, where inference latency adds to loop delay and excessive delays can degrade closed-loop performance or destabilize the system, compromising safety ( Shin & Cui, 1995 ; Findeisen & Allgöwer, 2004 ; Ma et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Nan et al., 2026 ) .

To address memory constraints, existing compression methods use quantization ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , distillation ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , pruning ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , and low-rank factorization ( Hsu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . Varying memory budgets across edge devices call for elastic compression of a single trained checkpoint to multiple model sizes. SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) enables such elastic compression by learning sparse-and-low-rank (SLR) representations for each linear projection 1 1 1 Here, linear projection refers to a learned linear map in the attention (query/key/value/output) or multi-layer perceptron (MLP; up/gate/down) modules. Embeddings and the language model head are excluded unless noted. during pretraining. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into lower inference latency. Unstructured SLR saves static memory but incurs higher inference latency (see Appendix A.1 ). We identify the overhead from irregular memory access in unstructured sparse operations as a critical barrier to deploying large models on edge devices. Hardware-friendly patterns, including block sparsity ( Okanovic et al., 2025 ) , N : M N\!:\!M sparsity ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , and row-/column-wise sparsity ( Wen et al., 2016 ) , are therefore required to translate these memory savings into efficient edge inference. A straightforward extension of SALAAD is to impose these patterns on its learned sparse components after pretraining. However, our experiments show that this post-hoc conversion can sharply degrade model performance (see Appendix A.2 ). We therefore induce structured sparsity during pretraining , allowing the SLR components to adapt jointly to the structural constraints.

To this end, we introduce S-SALAAD ( S tructured- S parse- A nd- L ow-Rank A daptation via AD MM), a plug-and-play framework that learns structured SLR representations during pretraining for elastic compression and efficient edge inference. Based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), it induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture or optimizer update rules. Efficient low-rank updates reduce pretraining overhead, while budget-aware refinement enables zero-shot compression of a single checkpoint to multiple parameter budgets without calibration data or further training. Among these patterns, we identify block sparsity as a practical choice for elastic deployment given current technical capabilities. With dedicated CPU and GPU kernels, the resulting models advance the perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier relative to the evaluated baselines. Our contributions are summarized as follows: ❖ A plug-and-play framework for structured-sparsity learning. S-SALAAD jointly learns model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components under the task loss, adapting the representation to structural constraints during pretraining. S-SALAAD induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture, and it is compatible with existing optimizers.

❖ A practical end-to-end implementation. To support the training of larger models and their edge deployment, we address bottlenecks in the training, compression, and inference stages. Specifically, we use i) a warm-started iterative singular value decomposition (I-SVD) to reduce the computational overhead of low-rank updates during pretraining ii) energy-guided alternating refinement (EGAR) to enable zero-shot compression without calibration data or further training, allocating the parameter budget across projections without a preset sparse–low-rank split and reducing reconstruction error within the allocated capacities iii) dedicated CPU and GPU kernels to exploit the induced structured sparsity and reduce inference latency . ❖ Empirical Pareto frontier across training settings. S-SALAAD advances the empirical perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier across hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines, with each checkpoint supporting multiple compression budgets. These gains hold for Llama2-1B pretraining and cross-architecture distillation from Nemotron-3-Super-120B to Qwen3-1.7B. ❖ Analysis of structured representations. S-SALAAD provides an explicit structured representation of Transformer weights, enabling us to identify distinct sparsity characteristics across linear projection types. Our analysis identifies block sparsity as a practical choice for advancing the perplexity-memory-latency Pareto frontier, combining flexible compression with efficient execution on CPUs and GPUs. Furthermore, we also reveal the relationship between tolerable block granularity and model scale, providing empirical guidance for selecting block sizes when extending S-SALAAD to larger models.

Quality evaluation. Except for the separately sourced LORO reference described below, perplexity is measured on held-out tokens of the training corpus—C4 for Llama and FineWeb-Edu for Qwen3-1.7B—under the corresponding evaluation protocol. Perplexities are compared within each model family, not across the two corpora. We evaluate zero-shot downstream accuracy on ARC-Easy, OpenBookQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, PIQA, and SciQ using the LM Evaluation Harness ( Gao et al., 2024 ) . Baseline implementations and profiling. Vanilla training and SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) provide training references, while the L L -only special case ( S ≡ 0 S\equiv 0 ) provides a reference for block granularity. EGAR produces variants at multiple parameter budgets from each S-SALAAD checkpoint without calibration data. All compressed models are evaluated without additional fine-tuning for fair comparison. For Wanda and SparseGPT, we use the measured latency and throughput of the corresponding dense models, as the evaluated hardware lacks native acceleration for : 4 2\!:\!4 sparsity. This illustrates that the latency benefits of a sparsity pattern are constrained by support from the target hardware. We use the SVD-LLM V2 implementation ( Wang et al., 2025b ) for the SVD-LLM baseline. For LORO, we use its published Llama-1B perplexity of 15.19 at rank 512 after training on 13.1B C4 tokens ( Mo et al., 2025 ) . We profile its deployment form locally by replacing the seven projections in each layer of our Llama-1B backbone with pairs of rank-512 linear factors, retaining dense embeddings and the output head. This backbone uses FFN width 5632, compared with 5461 in the published LORO model, so the combined quality–cost point serves as an external reference.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix B B than for the down-projection matrix A A . However, the ratio η B / η A \eta_{B}/\eta_{A} itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal–noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard Init[A] , the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for B B , η B \eta_{B} , the initialization scale β \beta , and the adapter rank r r . In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of 1 / n 1/n , stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 22 ] is a standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) [ 21 , 35 , 33 ] . Given a width- n n LoRA layer with pretrained weight W ∈ ℝ n × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and input Z ¯ ∈ ℝ n \underline{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , LoRA uses Z ¯ = W ​ Z ¯ + α r ​ B ​ A ​ Z ¯ \bar{Z}=W\underline{Z}+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\underline{Z} , where A ∈ ℝ r × n A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and B ∈ ℝ n × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} are trainable with learning rates (LRs) η A \eta_{A} and η B \eta_{B} . Here r ≪ n r\ll n is the adapter rank and α / r \alpha/r is the LoRA update multiplier. We use β \beta to denote the initialization-magnitude hyperparameter: standard LoRA initialization, denoted Init[A] , initializes B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 and initializes A 0 A_{0} randomly with mean zero and standard deviation β n − 1 / 2 \beta n^{-1/2} , so the adapter preserves the pretrained model output at step zero. Figure 1 : Overview of LoRA initialization and feature-norm stability. Left : LoRA branch notation and the initialization scalings compared in this work, including standard Init[A] , Init[AB] , and the proposed Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] . Right : feature-norm trajectories at width n = 4096 n=4096 for different initialization scales β \beta . Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] keeps the LoRA features nearly invariant to β \beta , while the alternative scalings exhibit stronger initialization-dependent growth.

Despite its simplicity, LoRA is sensitive to hyperparameters (HPs). The rank r r controls the expressive capacity of the adapter [ 60 ] , but its effect is inseparable from the update multiplier λ r = α / r \lambda_{r}=\alpha/r . Kalajdzievski [ 27 ] shows that the conventional choice α / r \alpha/r is not rank-stabilized: it can shrink adapter activations and gradients as r r grows, slowing learning at high ranks and motivating the alternative α / r \alpha/\sqrt{r} . LRs introduce a further source of brittleness. Recent empirical work shows that, after sufficiently broad LR sweeps, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants [ 32 ] . This shifts the practical question from only designing new adapters to understanding LoRA HP selection. LoRA+ [ 17 ] gives a principled route toward understanding LR selection by assigning different LRs to the two LoRA matrices. Its infinite-width feature learning analysis suggests that efficient LoRA feature updates require an asymmetric regime with η B ≫ η A \eta_{B}\gg\eta_{A} and, under idealized scaling assumptions, a ratio η B / η A ≈ n \eta_{B}/\eta_{A}\approx n . We write this ratio as ρ = η B / η A \rho=\eta_{B}/\eta_{A} . The asymmetric regime is attractive because B B directly controls the LoRA branch output, so increasing η B \eta_{B} can accelerate adaptation. In finite pretrained LLMs, however, ρ \rho often becomes another hyperparameter to tune: large ratios can improve performance, but under Init[A] they can also trigger instability. We address the gap between the theoretical LR guidance and practical LLM fine-tuning in this paper.

We show that the fragility of asymmetric LRs comes from an initialization-dependent noise term that survives even though the LoRA branch has zero output at initialization. Although B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 , the random matrix A 0 A_{0} affects the branch as soon as B B moves away from zero. A signal–noise decomposition of the LoRA feature update reveals two components: a task-driven signal from optimizer updates and a noise term from the interaction between the learned B B and the random initial A A . Both terms scale with η B \eta_{B} , so increasing η B \eta_{B} amplifies useful adaptation and initialization noise at the same time. In the small-LR regime common in pretrained LLM fine-tuning, the signal can remain controlled while the Init[A] noise contribution does not vanish with width, making large ρ \rho , large initialization scale β \beta , and large update multiplier α / r \alpha/r especially brittle.

We propose Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , a simple LoRA initialization that suppresses initialization-induced noise while preserving zero initial adapter output. The central mechanism is that standard Init[A] leaves a random initial projection in A A that is amplified as soon as B B moves; Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] reduces this term by one additional factor of width, making high-ratio asymmetric LRs much less brittle. Practically, this reduces best-ratio drift across initialization scales, lowers dependence on exhaustive HP sweeps, and improves robustness to large update multipliers ( α / r ) (\alpha/r) , enabling stronger updates and better performance on downstream tasks. These gains are consistent across the controlled HP-transfer experiment, encoder-only RoBERTa fine-tuning, and decoder-only LLM generation benchmarks. More broadly, the design philosophy only targets the scale of A 0 A_{0} rather than its distribution. It can therefore be applied to structured initializers: we compress the A 0 A_{0} scale of Orthogonal and EVA while retaining their selected directions, and use a factorwise gauge transformation for PiSSA that preserves its initialized low-rank product. In selected Llama arithmetic sweeps, these three variance-compressed variants remain stable under aggressive asymmetric LRs for which their uncompressed counterparts degrade ( Section E.3 ). This extension is empirical: the B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 theorem does not directly cover PiSSA, and we do not claim uniform gains over carefully tuned base initializers.

2610.30280:bd4bc9553ef8b97a8c1f1a2dd7c0b.question: What transformer or LLM experiments test PolarGD and Newton–Schulz Muon against AdamW, gradient descent, or other Muon variants? Report models, measured outcomes, learning-rate controls, and stated limits of transfer from matrix quadratics.

passages.text: Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW , yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD , the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon , on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

Existing analyses view these methods as non-Euclidean trust-region ( Kovalev, 2025 ) or LMO-based steepest descent ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) and provide convergence guarantees for Muon ( Li and Hong, 2025 ) . These are worst-case bounds over broad function classes, governed by smoothness constants in the chosen norm and by norm-equivalence factors; where they suggest an advantage over (stochastic) gradient descent ( GD ), it comes from comparing such constants across norms ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Davis and Drusvyatskiy, 2025 ) . They do not separate the effect of the orthogonalized direction from that of the step-size scale set by these constants, so when this direction improves on the gradient step remains open. Analyses of Muon with finite Newton--Schulz treat it as an approximation of the polar factor whose error worsens the guarantees ( Shulgin et al., 2026 ; Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Takezawa et al., 2026 ) , related work attributes this error to ill-conditioning and replaces the solver ( Refael et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) , and improved solvers aim to reduce it ( Cesista et al., 2025 ; Grishina et al., 2025 ; Amsel et al., 2026 ) .

We study this question on matrix quadratics. Quadratic models are the classical setting for understanding optimizers, and they have repeatedly explained optimizer behavior in deep learning, from critical batch sizes and the value of preconditioning ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) to the advantage of Adam on transformers ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and of sign descent under Zipf-distributed data ( Kunstner and Bach, 2025 ) . Their matrix-valued form already contains the features that matter for orthogonalized updates: singular structure, anisotropic curvature, dependence on initialization, and the choice of coordinate system. We focus on the core update of Muon and of the methods above, X k + 1 = X k − γ k ​ polar ​ ( ∇ f ​ ( X k ) ) X_{k+1}=X_{k}-\gamma_{k}\mathrm{polar}(\nabla f(X_{k})) , and compare it with GD and SignGD . We call this update PolarGD by analogy with SignGD : it replaces the gradient by its polar factor, as SignGD replaces it by its entrywise sign (it has also been called spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2016 ) ). Momentum and stochasticity are left out on purpose, so that the effect of the update direction can be isolated. To compare the three directions on equal footing, we let each take its best scalar step, computed by exact line search. This removes learning-rate tuning from the comparison, so that methods are compared through their directions rather than through step-size choices. On matrix quadratics, the resulting one-step decreases are available in closed form and show a tradeoff between how much a direction D D decreases the loss to first order, its gain ⟨ G , D ⟩ \langle G,D\rangle , and the curvature tr ⁡ ( D ⊤ ​ H ​ D ) \mathrm{tr}(D^{\top}HD) along it.

We isolated the geometry of the orthogonalized update shared by Muon and related matrix optimizers by analyzing PolarGD on matrix quadratics. PolarGD benefits from orthogonal equivariance and implicit preconditioning by the iterate, but it is not uniformly better than GD or SignGD : it is fast near row-isotropic iterates and slow near rank deficiency, where exact polar normalization overweights tiny singular values. Finite Newton--Schulz softens the update exactly there and can then converge faster than exact polar, so it is not merely an approximation of the polar factor. The trajectory results rely on the quadratic structure, but Proposition 1 only needs the curvature bounds ( 2 ), and equivariance and the softening by Newton--Schulz hold for any objective, including the momentum matrix that Muon orthogonalizes. Our transformer measurements show that the regime where exact polar and Newton--Schulz differ occurs in practice. This suggests treating the number of Newton--Schulz steps, or the damping level, as a design choice of the optimizer rather than only as an accuracy setting.

We compare the exact PolarGD update against the practical Muon update with q ∈ { 3 , 4 , 5 } q\in\{3,4,5\} Newton--Schulz steps to observe how tiny singular modes are handled. Newton--Schulz uses Muon ’s coefficients ( a , b , c ) = ( 3.4445 , − 4.7750 , 2.0315 ) (a,b,c)=(3.4445,-4.7750,2.0315) and the Frobenius normalization of the reference implementation, all methods use exact line search, and we run 10 10 iterations. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

Existing analyses view these methods as non-Euclidean trust-region ( Kovalev, 2025 ) or LMO-based steepest descent ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) and provide convergence guarantees for Muon ( Li and Hong, 2025 ) . These are worst-case bounds over broad function classes, governed by smoothness constants in the chosen norm and by norm-equivalence factors; where they suggest an advantage over (stochastic) gradient descent ( GD ), it comes from comparing such constants across norms ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Davis and Drusvyatskiy, 2025 ) . They do not separate the effect of the orthogonalized direction from that of the step-size scale set by these constants, so when this direction improves on the gradient step remains open. Analyses of Muon with finite Newton--Schulz treat it as an approximation of the polar factor whose error worsens the guarantees ( Shulgin et al., 2026 ; Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Takezawa et al., 2026 ) , related work attributes this error to ill-conditioning and replaces the solver ( Refael et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) , and improved solvers aim to reduce it ( Cesista et al., 2025 ; Grishina et al., 2025 ; Amsel et al., 2026 ) .

We study this question on matrix quadratics. Quadratic models are the classical setting for understanding optimizers, and they have repeatedly explained optimizer behavior in deep learning, from critical batch sizes and the value of preconditioning ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) to the advantage of Adam on transformers ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and of sign descent under Zipf-distributed data ( Kunstner and Bach, 2025 ) . Their matrix-valued form already contains the features that matter for orthogonalized updates: singular structure, anisotropic curvature, dependence on initialization, and the choice of coordinate system. We focus on the core update of Muon and of the methods above, X k + 1 = X k − γ k ​ polar ​ ( ∇ f ​ ( X k ) ) X_{k+1}=X_{k}-\gamma_{k}\mathrm{polar}(\nabla f(X_{k})) , and compare it with GD and SignGD . Momentum and stochasticity are left out on purpose, so that the effect of the update direction can be isolated. To compare the three directions on equal footing, we let each take its best scalar step, computed by exact line search. This removes learning-rate tuning from the comparison, so that methods are compared through their directions rather than through step-size choices. passages.text: Momentum is central to stochastic optimization in deep learning, including the training of large language models. Classical momentum methods typically rely on a fast exponential moving average (EMA) scheme, which discounts past gradients on a fixed timescale and may underweight older gradients that remain informative. This creates a trade-off between retaining long-term history and adapting to recent changes. We introduce Hybrid Momentum ( HyM ), which combines a linearly weighted average of past gradients with a geometrically discounted fast momentum. The former assigns weights proportional to the gradients’ iteration indices and retains a growing span of history, while the latter emphasizes recent gradients. This hybrid construction is modular and can be combined with adaptive preconditioning and other update transformations. In particular, we propose HyMUON , which applies Newton–Schulz orthogonalization to the hybrid direction. Illustrative examples and controlled experiments demonstrate the benefits of combining gradient information across these two timescales. Across image classification, machine translation, and language modeling, HyM and HyMUON match or improve upon strong baselines. HyMUON improves over Muon on IWSLT14, and in both the 100k- and 600k-step GPT-2 124M OpenWebText regimes. For LLaMA-1.3B pretraining on C4, HyMUON achieves a final validation loss of 2.777 2.777 , compared with 2.903 2.903 for Muon.

We compare HyMUON against Muon reproduced with the hyperparameters selected by Gu and Xie (2026) for LLaMA-1.3B/C4. We tune the HyMUON optimizer hyperparameters; Appendix F.6 gives the selected configuration. Training uses C4/en with document packing for 10k steps. HyMUON reaches validation loss 2.777 2.777 , compared with 2.903 2.903 for Muon (Figure 5 , top right). The corresponding perplexity curves are reported in Figure 16 in Appendix F.6 . Appendix G reports an additional evaluation of HyMUON on the modded-nanoGPT Track 3 benchmark.

This experiment compares HyMUON with Muon for LLaMA-1.3B pretraining on C4. We reproduce the Muon baseline reported in Table 2 of Gu and Xie [2026] using the training configuration in their Table 5 and Appendix B.1. Muon’s peak learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} follows that configuration. The model has 1.339B parameters, 24 layers, hidden size 2048, feed-forward size 5461, 32 attention heads, and a 32k vocabulary. C4/en is streamed with document packing and a t5-base tokenizer; each step contains 512 sequences of length 1024. Both methods train for 10,000 steps, 1,000 linear warmup steps, cosine decay to one tenth of the peak learning rate, gradient clipping at 1.0, and an evaluation on 10,017,216 validation tokens every 1,000 steps. Each method processes 5,242,880,000 input tokens. Muon uses the hyperparameters selected by Gu and Xie [2026] : five NS iterations, momentum 0.95, matrix and auxiliary learning rates 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , and weight decay 0.1. For HyMUON , we search the matrix and auxiliary learning rates, matrix momentum, mixing weight, the coefficient for the auxiliary second moment, and weight decay for each parameter group. The selected configuration uses matrix and auxiliary learning rates 3 × 10 − 2 3\times 10^{-2} , mixing weight 0.99, Muon momentum 0.95, coefficient for the auxiliary second moment 0.999, and weight decay 0.2 for each group. Both parameter groups are evaluated at their averaged iterates. At 10k steps, validation loss and perplexity are 2.903 2.903 and 18.221 18.221 for Muon, and 2.777 2.777 and 16.078 16.078 for HyMUON . Figure 16 shows the perplexity curves; they are the exponential of the loss curves in Figure 5 .

Figure 16: LLaMA-1.3B validation perplexity on C4 with document packing through 10k steps in the comparison against the reproduced Muon baseline. This is the exponential transform of the curves of validation loss in Figure 5 ; HyMUON is evaluated at its averaged iterate.

2610.29812:7683f110ceffab481ec4389660f40.question: In the SciFact claim-verification ablation, what were the exact retrieval budgets, gold-paper recall, verdict accuracy, statistical uncertainty, and citation-audit results for single-shot retrieval versus the ReAct agent? Were backbone and output format held fixed?

passages.text: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49–59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79–86% accuracy, a significant 17–24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers .

Language agents that search the biomedical literature are quickly becoming a default component of scientific assistants: they formulate queries, read abstracts, and return verdicts with citations ( Lála et al., 2023 ; Skarlinski et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2024 ) . The design space of such harnesses is large, but the empirical basis for choosing among designs is thin. Three questions arise for anyone building a literature agent for the life sciences: (i) Does giving a frontier model access to PubMed improve its verdicts over closed-book answering, or does parametric knowledge suffice? (ii) Is an agentic loop, in which the model writes and refines its own queries ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Nakano et al., 2021 ) , worth its additional cost over a fixed one-shot retrieval pipeline ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) ? (iii) When agents cite papers, are those citations faithful to what they actually read? We study these questions in a controlled setting: expert-written biomedical claim verification on SciFact ( Wadden et al., 2020 ) , using the live PubMed E-utilities API as the only tool. We hold the backbone model, prompt format, and output schema fixed and vary only the harness : closed-book, single-shot retrieval, a ReAct-style multi-query agent, and an oracle that receives the gold abstracts. We run the same protocol with two backbones and decompose errors into retrieval failures (the gold paper was never seen) and reasoning failures (the gold paper was seen but the verdict was wrong).

Retrieval and citation diagnostics. SciFact documents are identified by Semantic Scholar IDs, not PMIDs, so we map a retrieved PubMed record to a gold document by normalized title match (exact or ratio > 0.9 >0.9 ). Gold recall is the fraction of Support / Contradict claims for which at least one gold abstract was retrieved. For retrieval conditions, a citation is unfaithful if its PMID was never returned by the tool. For closed-book citations, we check (a) existence in PubMed, (b) whether it matches a gold paper, and (c) topical relevance, judged by a model from a different family ( qwen3.8-27b ) given the claim and the cited title and abstract. We apply the same relevance judge to agent citations for comparison.

Table 1 and Figure 1 summarize the results. We highlight five findings. F1: Naive one-shot retrieval does not help, and changes how the model fails. Issuing the claim itself as a PubMed query retrieves a gold abstract for only 6% of evidence-bearing claims (4/64 for both backbones). Given mostly off-target abstracts, both models abstain heavily: 59% and 70% of their predictions are NEI, against 36% NEI in the gold labels. Accuracy is unchanged or lower relative to closed-book (53.0 vs. 55.0 and 49.0 vs. 59.0; exact McNemar p = 0.89 p{=}0.89 and p = 0.24 p{=}0.24 ). Retrieval converts overconfident errors into abstentions rather than into correct verdicts. When the gold abstract was retrieved, both models were correct on all 4 such claims.

F2: Letting the model write its own queries triples gold recall and gives the best verdicts, but the gains are modest. The agentic harness raises gold recall to 19–20% and attains the highest accuracy (62.0 for both backbones) and macro-F1 (60.3 and 61.1) of the non-oracle harnesses. Its queries are short, entity-centric reformulations (e.g., “chenodeoxycholic acid energy expenditure” instead of the full claim), and they can repair misspellings in the claim ( “Chenodeosycholic” → \rightarrow “chenodeoxycholic” ), which silently break literal retrieval. In paired comparisons, however, the improvement is not statistically significant at N = 100 N{=}100 : agent vs. single-shot, 24 vs. 15 discordant claims ( p = 0.20 p{=}0.20 ) and 29 vs. 16 ( p = 0.07 p{=}0.07 ); agent vs. closed-book, 13 vs. 6 ( p = 0.17 p{=}0.17 ) and 11 vs. 8 ( p = 0.65 p{=}0.65 ). The direction is consistent across both backbones. F3: Agents under-use their search budget. Despite a budget of 4 searches, the agents issue 1.42 and 1.70 queries per claim on average and answer after a single search on 71% and 55% of claims; only 3% and 6% of claims use the full budget. Among evidence-bearing claims where the agent never saw a gold abstract, it still answered Support / Contradict correctly 75% of the time, suggesting that it draws on other relevant PubMed papers or on parametric knowledge. But it also abstains less on true NEI claims (33% and 42% NEI recall, versus 72% and 81% for single-shot). Budget use is therefore a clear axis for harness improvement, for example through a minimum-evidence criterion before answering.

F4: Retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Given the gold abstracts, the same models reach 86.0% and 79.0% accuracy (macro-F1 85.8 and 78.6), 24 and 17 points above the best realistic harness. Unlike the differences among realistic harnesses, this gap is highly significant (agent vs. oracle, 5 vs. 29 discordant claims, p < 10 − 4 p{<}10^{-4} ; 9 vs. 26, p = 0.006 p{=}0.006 ). The oracle also restores calibrated abstention (NEI recall 78% and 86%) without sacrificing Support / Contradict accuracy, so the models reason well over evidence once they are shown the right papers.

Retrieval and citation diagnostics. SciFact documents are identified by Semantic Scholar IDs, not PMIDs, so we map a retrieved PubMed record to a gold document by normalized title match (exact or ratio > 0.9 >0.9 ). Gold recall is the fraction of Support / Contradict claims for which at least one gold abstract was retrieved. For retrieval conditions, a citation is unfaithful if its PMID was never returned by the tool. For closed-book citations, we check (a) existence in PubMed, (b) whether it matches a gold paper, and (c) topical relevance, judged by a model from a different family ( qwen3.8-27b ) given the claim and the cited title and abstract. We apply the same relevance judge to agent citations for comparison.

Table 1 and Figure 1 summarize the results. We highlight five findings. F1: Naive one-shot retrieval does not help, and changes how the model fails. Issuing the claim itself as a PubMed query retrieves a gold abstract for only 6% of evidence-bearing claims (4/64 for both backbones). Given mostly off-target abstracts, both models abstain heavily: 59% and 70% of their predictions are NEI, against 36% NEI in the gold labels. Accuracy is unchanged or lower relative to closed-book (53.0 vs. 55.0 and 49.0 vs. 59.0; exact McNemar p = 0.89 p{=}0.89 and p = 0.24 p{=}0.24 ). Retrieval converts overconfident errors into abstentions rather than into correct verdicts. When the gold abstract was retrieved, both models were correct on all 4 such claims.

The agentic harness raises gold recall to 19–20% and attains the highest accuracy (62.0 for both backbones) and macro-F1 (60.3 and 61.1) of the non-oracle harnesses. In paired comparisons, however, the improvement is not statistically significant at N = 100 N{=}100 : agent vs. single-shot, 24 vs. 15 discordant claims ( p = 0.20 p{=}0.20 ) and 29 vs. 16 ( p = 0.07 p{=}0.07 ); agent vs. closed-book, 13 vs. 6 ( p = 0.17 p{=}0.17 ) and 11 vs. 8 ( p = 0.65 p{=}0.65 ). The direction is consistent across both backbones. F3: Agents under-use their search budget. Despite a budget of 4 searches, the agents issue 1.42 and 1.70 queries per claim on average and answer after a single search on 71% and 55% of claims; only 3% and 6% of claims use the full budget. Among evidence-bearing claims where the agent never saw a gold abstract, it still answered Support / Contradict correctly 75% of the time, suggesting that it draws on other relevant PubMed papers or on parametric knowledge. But it also abstains less on true NEI claims (33% and 42% NEI recall, versus 72% and 81% for single-shot). Budget use is therefore a clear axis for harness improvement, for example through a minimum-evidence criterion before answering.

F4: Retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Given the gold abstracts, the same models reach 86.0% and 79.0% accuracy (macro-F1 85.8 and 78.6), 24 and 17 points above the best realistic harness. Unlike the differences among realistic harnesses, this gap is highly significant (agent vs. oracle, 5 vs. 29 discordant claims, p < 10 − 4 p{<}10^{-4} ; 9 vs. 26, p = 0.006 p{=}0.006 ). The oracle also restores calibrated abstention (NEI recall 78% and 86%) without sacrificing Support / Contradict accuracy, so the models reason well over evidence once they are shown the right papers.

2610.32878:5b98957edf2e12efa65cfaef8c107.question: Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3, what compression ratios or parameter budgets are used, which SVD baselines are compared at matched budgets, and what are the measured perplexity and zero-shot accuracy results? Does the method change pretraining or only compress pretrained models?

passages.text: We evaluate KFAC-SVD against state-of-the-art methods across three LLM families: Mistral , Llama 3 , and Qwen3 . Table 2 details the results for all approaches under uniform compression rates (0.9, 0.7) and calibration sample count, with an additional line for our search-enhanced variant. KFAC-SVD consistently yields the lowest perplexity, with gains most pronounced on Llama 3 . At a 0.7 compression ratio, KFAC-SVD improves perplexity on WikiText2 by 49 % over the best baseline ( DOBI-SVD ), extending to 66 % with LEMS . Zero-shot accuracy largely follows this trend: under mild compression (0.9), KFAC-SVD avoids the sharp accuracy drop seen in several baselines and stays in the mid- 50 s, while LEMS recovers near-lossless performance ( 61.8 % vs. 63.3 % original). Strictly comparing to prior Fisher-based methods, KFAC-SVD outperforms the baselines by up to 10.3 p.p. without the addition of LEMS . GFWSVD degrades significantly under identical conditions, reaffirming its conditioning challenges. The only exception is Mistral at 0.9, where ASVD achieves a slightly higher zero-shot accuracy (+0.35 p.p. ) despite worse perplexity. This implies Mistral relies on features well-aligned with activation magnitude, favoring simpler proxies in uniform settings. Overall, KFAC-SVD provides the most effective decomposition, especially when compared with other Fisher-based methods, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in the vast majority of evaluated settings.

To assess the scalability of LEMS , we evaluate the Qwen3 family (4B-32B) across five compression ratios (0.5-0.9). To demonstrate that LEMS is agnostic to a particular decomposition objective, we report results for both KFAC-SVD and the activation-based SVD-LLM . Figure 2 contrasts uniform allocation (solid) to LEMS (dashed), with numerical results provided in Supplement D .

Across all budgets and model sizes, LEMS consistently improves both perplexity and downstream utility. Averaged over ratios and models, it reduces perplexity by 17% for KFAC-SVD and 34% for SVD-LLM , while increasing zero-shot accuracy by +7.2 and +9.1 p.p. , respectively. Gains are largest under aggressive compression: at 0.5, LEMS cuts perplexity by ∼ \sim 26% ( KFAC-SVD ) / ∼ \sim 57% ( SVD-LLM ) on average and recovers +4.8 / +8.7 p.p. accuracy. Crucially, it also resolves the sharp accuracy dips observed in Qwen3 -32B under uniform allocation for both decompositions. The benefits extend beyond Qwen3 : on the substantially larger Llama 3 .1-70B, LEMS reduces WikiText2 perplexity from 7.9 to 4.5 and increases accuracy from 62.6 to 66.6 (see Supplement B.6 ). Comparing decompositions methods, KFAC-SVD achieves approximately 26% lower perplexity than SVD-LLM under uniform allocation, demonstrating stronger alignment with the downstream loss. When combined with LEMS , perplexities become tightly matched between the two methods, with SVD-LLM retaining a marginal edge in zero-shot accuracy ( ∼ \sim 0.3 p.p. ). Notably, the larger gains observed for SVD-LLM with LEMS suggest that suboptimal rank allocation is often a primary source of degradation under uniform compression. Differently, through the calibrated layer-wise error model and global ILP optimization, LEMS overcomes the degradation of uniform compression yielding consistent gains.

2610.33846:9858ac15869478917bfacff997767.question: Which CIFAR-10 models, noise rates, training controls, and test-error measurements support the claim that early stopping becomes unnecessary after random labels are fitted? What assumptions limit the kernel-gradient-flow phase diagram, and how do its regimes compare with the deep-network experiments?

passages.section: When is early stopping beneficial under label noise? A phase diagram for kernel gradient flow
passages.text: Fabrizio Boncoraglio Lenka Zdeborová 1 Statistical Physics of Computation Laboratory, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) CH-1015 Lausanne

Early stopping is commonly used to prevent fitting label noise from degrading generalization. Does this mean that, when a positive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable, the best test error must occur before interpolation? Experiments on a CIFAR10 classification task with randomly labeled examples motivate the opposite possibility: although fixed-feature and shallow models exhibit late-time deterioration of the test error, the need for early stopping essentially disappears in larger, deeper convolutional networks even after the random labels have all been classified correctly. We determine when late-time deterioration disappears entirely in a solvable setting. For kernel gradient flow on a synthetic noisy classification task, we derive sharp high-dimensional learning curves and obtain a phase diagram controlled by the balance between the linear kernel component that learns the shared relation between inputs and labels and the higher-order components that enable fitting the label noise. In one regime, generalization is optimized at finite time and early stopping is necessary. In another, generalization improves until interpolation, but the endpoint is suboptimal across kernels. At the boundary, the interpolating endpoint attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, even with extensive irreducible label noise, interpolation can outperform early stopping. The neural-network experiments leave open how learned representations acquire an analogous favorable geometry.

Figure 1: Generalization along the path to memorization. Test error on 2000 cats and dogs ( x x -axes) versus classification error on the randomly labelled automobiles ( y y -axes) taken from the CIFAR10 dataset. The fixed training set has n = 7000 n=7000 images: 2800 2800 cats, 2800 2800 dogs with their respective labels, and 1400 1400 automobiles with independent random labels. Panels vary the overparametrization ratio κ = P / n ≈ 1 , 10 , 100 \kappa=P/n\approx 1,10,100 , where P P counts optimized parameters. Curves average about 30 completed seeds; a centered arithmetic average of up to seven neighboring recorded times is applied to both coordinates for display, preserving the initial and final values. These parametric curves trace the two errors as training time t t increases. Triangles mark initialization, squares the last iterate and crosses the minimum displayed test error. All trainable networks use square loss and constant-rate Nesterov SGD, without augmentation or weight decay, through 1500 epochs; RF-CNN uses full-batch readout GD through 10 12 10^{12} steps. In Appendix F we provide all numerical details and the unsmoothed trajectories, including training loss.

We derive exact learning curves and obtain a phase diagram with three regimes, corresponding to three families of kernels. In the first, test error reaches its minimum at finite time and subsequently increases, so early stopping is necessary. In the second, test error improves until convergence, but the resulting interpolating predictor is suboptimal relative to other kernel geometries. Precisely at the boundary between these regimes, gradient flow converges to an interpolating predictor that attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel families and all training times. Thus, even in the presence of extensive label noise, interpolation can lead to a better test error than any early stopping. The kernel analysis therefore produces the behavior that motivated this work. At the critical geometry, the best test error is attained at interpolation, and the corresponding trajectory in Figure 4 closely resembles those of the larger, deeper neural networks in Figure 1 , whose best test performance is attained after all randomly labelled examples have been classified correctly. The theory thus provides a concrete realization of the observed phenomenon. It does not, however, explain how neural-network training constructs a representation with analogous properties. Determining which aspects of feature learning, model size, and architecture produce this behavior remains an open question.

In this work, we asked whether the presence of extensive label noise necessarily makes early stopping preferable to interpolation. The noisy CIFAR10 experiments in Fig. 1 and Appendix F support the hypothesis that deep and highly overparameterized neural networks actually do not benefit from early stopping. Figure 1 shows that the larger and deeper networks attain their best observed test performance only after their memorization error reaches zero, while fixed-feature and shallower models exhibit late-time test-error deterioration. Appendix F shows that this observation is robust beyond the setting of Fig. 1 : it persists across a range of training recipes, including cross-entropy, data augmentation, and a scheduled learning rate, as well as across additional optimization controls. We then asked whether the absence of a benefit from early stopping can be reproduced in an analytically solvable setting. Our analysis of high-dimensional learning curves for kernel gradient flow shows that it can. Kernel geometry determines whether the lowest test error occurs at a finite time or at convergence. We identify a critical kernel geometry for which the interpolating predictor attains the lowest test error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, fitting unpredictable labels need not come at the expense of generalization, in a sense yet considerably stronger than the one known from the literature on benign overfitting.

The critical-kernel trajectory provides a concrete fixed-representation counterpart of the behavior observed in the deeper neural networks: fitting the unpredictable labels does not produce a late-time deterioration of generalization, and the best test error is attained at the end of the trajectory. Our analysis does not, however, establish that the networks learn this same geometry, nor does it explain how feature learning, architecture, and optimization produce the empirically observed behavior. The theory nevertheless places the empirical hypothesis formulated in the introduction on a precise footing: even under extensive label noise, the absence of a benefit from early stopping is possible and can be controlled by representation geometry. Understanding how larger and deeper feature-learning architectures realize analogous behavior remains an open question. All the results can be reproduced using the code provided in the repository: https://github.com/SPOC-group/Early-stopping .

2610.31897:495674a7fb48beba3495985a05608.question: In the Llama2-1B pretraining experiments, what are the exact peak GPU training memory, training time or throughput, and validation perplexity for S-SALAAD versus vanilla training and SALAAD under the same model, tokens, and hardware? At matched compressed parameter budgets, what are the perplexity, model memory, and inference latency versus SVD-LLM V2?

passages.text: We pretrain Llama2 models (1B and 350M) on C4 ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) and distill Nemotron-3-Super-120B into Qwen3-1.7B on FineWeb-Edu ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) . Dataset and model details are provided in Appendix D.2 , and training settings in Appendix D.3 . We compare against Wanda ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , SparseGPT ( Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ) , SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , SVD-LLM ( Wang et al., 2025c ) , LORO ( Mo et al., 2025 ) , vanilla training, and SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) . LOST ( Li et al., 2025 ) is excluded because it requires changes to the underlying model architecture. We evaluate perplexity, zero-shot downstream accuracy, peak memory, and prefill inference latency. To assess deployment under different memory and compute constraints, we profile inference on Quadro RTX 6000 and RTX 2080 Ti GPUs and 4 × \times AMD EPYC 7662 CPU hosts. Baseline implementations and evaluation protocols are detailed in Appendices D.4 and D.5 .

Quality evaluation. Except for the separately sourced LORO reference described below, perplexity is measured on held-out tokens of the training corpus—C4 for Llama and FineWeb-Edu for Qwen3-1.7B—under the corresponding evaluation protocol. Perplexities are compared within each model family, not across the two corpora. We evaluate zero-shot downstream accuracy on ARC-Easy, OpenBookQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, PIQA, and SciQ using the LM Evaluation Harness ( Gao et al., 2024 ) . Baseline implementations and profiling. Vanilla training and SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) provide training references, while the L L -only special case ( S ≡ 0 S\equiv 0 ) provides a reference for block granularity. EGAR produces variants at multiple parameter budgets from each S-SALAAD checkpoint without calibration data. All compressed models are evaluated without additional fine-tuning for fair comparison. 2610.28072:a663e9cd4b25b1997aaa5b2a79ded.question: For MuPACE on 64 LoRA fine-tuning problems and Qwen3-32B or Qwen3.8-27B, how were fixed schedules and Muon baselines tuned and matched for runs or compute? What measured gains remain against per-task tuned peaks, and what are the meta-training and inference overheads?

passages.text: Learning rate schedules are typically fixed before training begins, yet when fine-tuning large language models with low-rank adapters (LoRA), the appropriate scale varies substantially with the model, task, and adapter configuration. Practitioners re-tune a schedule for every new problem, yet a tuned schedule still cannot react to the training dynamics it encounters. We instead amortize learning rate selection across LoRA fine-tuning problems. We leave the base optimizer, Muon, untouched, so that its normalized update fixes the direction, and meta-learn only the global step size. Our method MuPACE is a small recurrent policy, meta-trained across a distribution of fine-tuning runs, that conditions on the observed trajectory and emits bounded adjustments to an interpretable analytic schedule. On 64 fine-tuning problems, MuPACE outperforms standard fixed schedules at a strong shared default on 64–78% of problems and is on par with the same schedules with per-task tuned peaks. Meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, MuPACE transfers one-shot to unseen tasks on models as deep as 64 layers, such as Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, where a single run remains competitive with swept schedules.

We therefore ask the following question: Can learning rate schedule selection instead be amortized across LoRA fine-tuning problems? We introduce MuPACE ( Mu on P olicy for A daptive C ontrol across LoRA Fine-tuning E pisodes), a learned, trajectory-conditioned learning rate scheduler for LoRA. LoRA fine-tuning is especially relevant because only a few large organizations train large language models from scratch, while most users adapt existing pretrained models ( Bommasani et al., 2021 ) . Unlike previous learned optimizers that meta-learn the update rule itself ( Metz et al., 2022b ; Moudgil et al., 2025 ) , we leave Muon unchanged and meta-learn only its global step-size schedule. A small recurrent policy observes the optimization trajectory and predicts bounded modifications to an analytic schedule family, explicitly separating changes in overall scale from changes in schedule shape. The scheduler is meta-trained across a distribution of fine-tuning episodes and then applied one-shot to new problems, producing an adaptive schedule within a single training run without hyperparameter search or downstream-specific tuning.

To assess the effectiveness of our approach, we evaluate whether a single meta-trained scheduler can replace per-task learning rate search across a broad range of fine-tuning settings, spanning pretrained models, downstream tasks, adapter configurations, batch sizes, and training horizons. On 64 problems, MuPACE outperforms strong fixed defaults on 64–78% of tasks and performs on par with schedules tuned separately for each problem, while requiring only a single trial. Moreover, despite being meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, MuPACE generalizes in a one-shot manner to large-scale models such as Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B (both with 64 layers) on unseen downstream tasks. It achieves competitive performance close to that of swept schedules while requiring only a single run. Our key contributions are: • We introduce MuPACE , a meta-learned, trajectory-conditioned learning rate scheduler for LoRA fine-tuning that adapts a bounded analytic schedule while leaving the base optimizer, Muon, unchanged, enabling one-shot application without target-task learning rate search. • We show that a single meta-trained scheduler generalizes across fine-tuning problems and model scales. On 64 problems, MuPACE outperforms strong fixed defaults and performs comparably to per-task tuned schedules, while transferring one-shot to Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B on unseen tasks, where it remains competitive with tuned learning rate schedules in a single run.

passages.section: H2: Meta-learned schedulers can eliminate per-task learning rate search while retaining competitive performance on in-distribution fine-tuning problems.
passages.text: We repeat the H1 comparison against the per-task tuned baselines, comparing their validation-based learning rate search with our learned scheduler, which requires no per-task sweep. Sign tests are applied as in H1. Figure 3 shows that the learned scheduler approaches the performance of per-task tuned schedules without the cost of a learning rate sweep. Our learned scheduler wins on 44 % 44\% , 45 % 45\% , and 38 % 38\% of draws against tuned cosine, WSD, and constant, with median relative differences of − 0.28 % -0.28\% , − 0.24 % -0.24\% , and − 0.90 % -0.90\% . None of these win rates differs significantly from 50 % 50\% . Per-task tuning matters here as the best peak varies by roughly a factor of five across the baselines. To quantify how much of that tuning the learned scheduler makes unnecessary, we take the draws where tuning lowers test loss by at least 0.5 % 0.5\% over the default and measure the fraction of that gain the learned scheduler achieves in one run, ( L default − L learned ) / ( L default − L tuned ) (L_{\mathrm{default}}-L_{\mathrm{learned}})/(L_{\mathrm{default}}-L_{\mathrm{tuned}}) . The median recovery is 80 % 80\% , 83 % 83\% and 78 % 78\% against cosine, WSD and constant (Figure 5 ). Figure 3: Learned scheduler versus validation-tuned baselines on 64 64 tasks. (a) Win rates and Holm-adjusted sign-test p p values. (b) Relative test-loss reduction versus each tuned baseline, where positive favors learned. Dots show tasks, diamonds medians, and bars interquartile ranges. Figure 4: Learning rate applied by the learned scheduler on 16 16 of the 64 64 in-distribution tasks. Figure 5: Median fraction of the per-task tuning gain recovered by the learned scheduler in one run, on the draws where tuning improves test loss by at least 0.5 % 0.5\% .

passages.section: H3: Meta-learned schedulers can transfer one-shot to out-of-distribution fine-tuning problems, avoiding per-task learning rate search while retaining competitive performance.
passages.text: Figure 6 evaluates MuPACE on models and datasets that were both unseen during policy training, comparing a single MuPACE run against fixed schedules with the peak tuned by a five-trial sweep on each dataset. The tuned baselines reach slightly lower test loss, with median relative differences of 1.13 % 1.13\% – 2.43 % 2.43\% on Qwen3-32B and 2.59 % 2.59\% – 3.02 % 3.02\% on Qwen3.8-27B, and MuPACE wins on 2 2 of 8 8 datasets per model. This gap is the price of one run versus five. Given only one trial, the fixed schedules perform worse than MuPACE by 14 % 14\% – 18 % 18\% on average and need two to three trials to reach the same performance (Appendix C ). Against Hypergradient Descent, the other sweep-free method, MuPACE achieves lower test loss on every dataset for both models, whether Hypergradient Descent is used with or without μ \mu P post-scaling. Figure 6: MuPACE versus validation-tuned baselines and Hypergradient Descent on (a) Qwen3-32B and (b) Qwen3.8-27B. Values show baseline minus MuPACE test loss (positive favors MuPACE).

We ask whether MuPACE still outperforms the fixed schedules when the latter are given the same depth-dependent scaling and their learning-rate peaks are selected without any target-task search. Specifically, we apply the learned policy’s depth- μ \mu P multiplier from Equation 6 to cosine, WSD, and constant schedules on both out-of-distribution models. For each schedule family, we transfer (i) the default peak of 10 − 3 10^{-3} and (ii) the best fixed peak from a sweep on the in-distribution evaluation, denoted p ∗ p^{*} . For WSD and constant, the source-selected and default peaks coincide. Thus, the comparison tests whether MuPACE provides gains beyond transferring either default or source-tuned depth-scaled fixed schedules. All arms report test loss at their own best-validation checkpoint. MuPACE outperforms every depth-scaled fixed control on every dataset of both models except default-peak cosine on GSM8K for Qwen3-32B (Figure 14 ). This supports gains beyond applying the same depth-scaling rule to default or source-tuned fixed schedules without target-task search. Figure 14: Depth-scaled fixed schedules versus MuPACE on Qwen3-32B (left) and Qwen3.8-27B (right). Positive differences favor the learned policy. Target-tuned schedules and Hypergradient Descent are shown for context. Depth-scaled fixed schedules use no target-task peak selection.
